description.content: A story about the early internet, the Flash community, and the excitement of building a company around a new creative language that was still being invented.

content: What inspired us when we started [Monks][https://www.monks.com]? I think it came from three things:

This is the late 90s in the Netherlands, in Amsterdam. I'm studying communications in 1996-1997. You start seeing the Internet become sort of a consumer-level thing, and of course it felt very disconnected from what we were learning in school when it came to communication. Schools are always going to be a little slower when it comes to this type of technological shift. The initial excitement was: 'Hey, there's this new thing, and you can make things for it! You can connect with people on it." It just felt so exciting.

I think those three things combined were the inspiration: the internet as a new channel, the early Flash community, and then coming together in a company/community/culture that shares that excitement of making amazing things.
We invited Wesley because [Monks][https://www.monks.com] was one of those references that helped us understand how far a digital company could go.

For many of us building from outside the main centers of the industry, [Monks][https://www.monks.com] represented something powerful: a studio that started from curiosity, craft, and experimentation, and grew into a global creative force without losing its connection to the culture of making.

Wesley inspired us not only through the work, but through the way he speaks about the industry: with clarity, perspective, and a deep understanding of how technology, creativity, people, and culture come together.

His story makes that even more meaningful. It goes back to a moment when the internet was becoming a new channel, Flash was unlocking new creative possibilities, and a whole community was inventing a language in real time.
That spirit shaped a generation of digital studios, including us.

For [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], [Monks][https://www.monks.com] was always more than a company to admire. It was proof that a group of people excited about making amazing things could build a culture, a business, and eventually a global impact.
That is why Wesley had to be part of this archive. Because some people do not just build companies. They help define what an entire industry believes is possible.

title: The phone call I didn't expect

description.content: I almost didn't become a designer. Not because I lacked the talent or the drive, but because I was 18 years old, standing outside a restaurant in London on my first day of work, completely overwhelmed.

content: I had just left Latvia to study Graphic Design in one of the most demanding cities in the world. And to survive there, I needed a job. So there I was, in my waitress uniform, staring at the door, thinking: why the hell am I doing this?

Home was comfortable. Home was safe. London was hard and loud and unfamiliar, and in that moment, all I wanted was permission to quit. So I did what any strong, independent woman would do. I called my mum. Because my mum is the warmest person in the world, and I knew she would tell me it was okay to come home.
But my dad picked up.
A man of few words. Always the pointiest ones.

I told him everything: how hard it was, how much I was struggling, how I wasn't sure I could do it. And I waited for that permission to quit. Instead, he told me that when he was 18, he was being forced into the Soviet Army (at that time Latvia was part of it), leaving behind his pregnant wife, with no choice and no way home. And then he asked me, simply: "Why do you want to quit before you've even tried? It was your dream to study in London."
That was it. No comfort. No softness. Just a perspective check that hit me like a fast train.

I put the phone in my pocket, walked through that door, and worked my first shift. I stayed. I studied. I graduated. And it turned out I was an almost impressively bad waitress, but that's beside the point.
The second time I faced that same crossroads, the stakes felt even higher.

It was 2015. I had just joined .[Monks][https://www.monks.com] as a designer, a big global company unlike anything I had worked at before. I had worked at a smaller agency back in Latvia, but this was a different world entirely. Leading brands. World-class talent everywhere I looked. And me, drowning quietly in imposter syndrome, convinced that absolutely everyone around me was better, smarter, more deserving of their seat.

Then one Friday afternoon, a designer sitting next to me began packing up his things. I made small talk and asked if he was starting his weekend early. He turned to me and said: "I'm an award-winning designer, and I have my own agenda, unlike you."

He probably had a bad day. I hope he did. But those words landed on someone already carrying more self-doubt than she could hold. I went home, sat at my kitchen table, and started looking up flights back to Latvia while writing my resignation letter in my head.
And then I flashed back. Outside that restaurant. My dad's voice.
Why do you want to quit before you've even tried?

I still had the choice. I could leave, or I could stay and learn from the best, push myself further than I had ever gone, and find out what I was actually capable of. I chose to stay. And not long after, my Creative Director handed me a brief with the words: "Let's see if you swim or drown."
I swam. I pushed the work further than I thought I could. And I created one of the best pieces of my career, born entirely from a mix of self-doubt and sheer determination not to give up again.

What I understand now is that inspiration rarely arrives as a grand gesture. Sometimes it is a pointed question from a father who picks up the phone when you needed your mum. Sometimes it is a moment of humiliation that sends you home, only to send you back stronger the next morning.

The choice to stay, both times, made me who I am. And I have learned that the most powerful thing anyone can do for another person is refuse to let them quit on themselves, even when that refusal feels, in the moment, like the opposite of kindness.

That is what I carry with me. Into every project. Every team. Every conversation with someone standing 'outside their version of a restaurant', wondering if they are good enough to walk through the door.
We invited Liva because every time our paths crossed, something about the way she thinks, speaks, and stands for her work stayed with us.

There is a calm strength in her presence. A clarity and conviction that do not need to be loud to be powerful. Whether through her time at MediaMonks, Code d’Azur, or the new chapters she continues to build, Liva has always carried her work with consistency, integrity, and a very clear point of view.
What inspires us is not only the quality of the projects, but the way she shows up: with depth, honesty, and a strong sense of what design can mean when it is led with intention.

Her story makes that even clearer. It speaks about doubt, resilience, and the moments when someone refuses to let you quit before you have even tried. And it shows how those moments can become part of the way we later lead, support, and challenge others.

Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we learned that inspiration often comes from people who quietly raise the standard. People whose presence, perspective, and way of moving through the industry make others want to do better.
Liva is one of those people.

title: Three stories about momentum, roles and failure

description.content: Some people inspire us not only because of what they have done, but because of the way they see the world. Fernando Vega Olmos is one of them.

content: A creative, strategist, communicator, and one of the most influential figures in Argentine and Latin American advertising, Fernando has something difficult to explain: the ability to turn a small anecdote into a powerful idea.

In these three stories, he talks about difficulties, roles, failure, and craft. But above all, he talks about a way of moving through life: with clarity, humor, depth, and a strong belief in the transformative power of what may first appear to be a limitation.
A story about how a personal difficulty can become a tool, a perspective, and eventually, a craft.

Fernando talks about childhood, words, and the alternative paths we find to say what we want to say. And within that journey, a powerful idea appears: sometimes, the thing that makes us most uncomfortable is exactly what pushes us to find our own voice.
A scene witnessed more than thirty years ago becomes a lesson about teams, roles, and responsibility.
Each person has a place to occupy for something to happen. And when someone is not doing what they are there to do, it is not only their part that stops: the whole thing stops.
A simple, almost street-level story that ends up saying something much bigger about leadership, collaboration, and focus.
Through the story of Camille Pissarro and the Impressionists, Fernando reflects on failure, rejection, and persistence.

Not as an empty “never give up” kind of epic, but from a much deeper perspective: understanding that many true shifts are born at the margins, far from immediate validation, and that failure can also become a way of building character, work, and future.
We invited Fernando because, long before we knew him personally, he had already inspired us.

We first heard him speak live at the FePI Awards in 2016, and something stayed with us. It was not only what he said, but how he said it: with clarity, confidence, impact, and a very personal way of explaining complex ideas without stripping them of their depth.

Since then, his way of thinking about creativity, communication, and the profession has been a constant reference. Fernando has that rare ability to bring together strategic thinking, human sensitivity, and narrative power. To turn a phrase into a lesson. An anecdote into a compass. A difficulty into a force.

title: Moment of inspiration: a story from Intermedia

content: We were putting together the merger of two companies: he was an internet provider, and I had a Lotus Notes consulting firm for the financial market.
That day, my then future partner asked me to meet outside the office because he wanted to talk.
Sitting in front of two cups of coffee, next to a sunny window in downtown Buenos Aires, he said:
—We won’t be able to partner. It’s not viable. Lotus Notes and Netscape are going to compete in service delivery.
I had just gotten divorced, I had three children to raise, and I needed to work.
The merger was vital.
Terrified, and without understanding the technical explanation, I recovered for a moment my teenage boldness and replied:
—Let’s expand the offering of email platforms. We have to sell Lotus, Netscape, and Microsoft too.
Martin looked at me, confused.
My proposal, although somewhat illogical, was brave.
A week later, we signed the contract for the new company.
That desperate answer, that moment, shaped the way I worked for the next 30 years: always being at the service of clients and moving at the rhythm of the market.
Today, we no longer have that company. We sold it.
Today, Netscape and Lotus Notes are part of history.
Today, I no longer work at that company.

Today, I remember that moment of inspiration as the one that marked my professional and personal life forever: to look for alternatives, look ahead, and not become disillusioned even when I am disappointed.
We invited Luciana because she was part of our first real professional chapter.

Before [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], before the studio, and before many of the lessons that came later, there was Intermedia: the place where Lucas first understood what it meant to work with a brief, meet a delivery date, receive feedback, start over, and take responsibility for a process.

Luciana inspired us because that stage taught us something fundamental: design is not only talent or intuition. It is also commitment, responsibility, method, and the ability to sustain the work even when the context demands more from you.
Her story connects deeply with that. It speaks about a defining moment, a decision made in the middle of fear, and the ability to find an alternative when everything seemed to be closing down.

Looking for options, looking ahead, and not becoming disillusioned even when one is disappointed. That way of moving through uncertainty was part of what we learned in our first contact with the professional world.
That is why we wanted Luciana to be part of this archive. Because some people do not only give you a first opportunity: they also show you, through action, what it means to work seriously.

description.content: A reflection on building from curiosity, proving that a global studio can be born far from the obvious places, and learning that meaningful growth takes longer than we think.

content: In this video, Uros looks back at the early days of [Flow Ninja][https://www.flowninja.com/], when the company was still small, ambitious, and just beginning to find its place in the global web industry.

What started as curiosity —a desire to build websites his own way, work with great clients, and explore what a studio could become— slowly turned into something much bigger: a global organization, a family business in the deepest sense, and a path that changed not only his career, but the lives of the people around him.

He also speaks openly about something many founders rarely talk about: the loneliness of building. The pressure of being a solo founder, the moments when nothing seems to work, and the need to keep going even when the results are not visible yet.
But perhaps the most powerful lesson is the one he would give to anyone just starting out: give yourself a longer time horizon.
Things may take twice, three times, or five times longer than expected. But if the vision is real, and you keep showing up for it, the journey becomes worth it.
We invited Uros because watching what he has built with [Flow Ninja][https://www.flowninja.com/] has been genuinely inspiring.

From the first time we met, there was a clarity and energy around him that stayed with us. He was not just building another studio. He was building with conviction, with a strong point of view, and with a clear desire to own his space in the Webflow ecosystem.

What inspires us is not only the growth itself, but the way he made it happen: with focus, positioning, ambition, and a deep belief that great work can come from places that are not always seen as obvious centers of opportunity.
Uros represents a kind of founder energy we deeply admire: curious, driven, resilient, and willing to keep pushing even when the path is lonely or uncertain.

Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we learned that inspiration often travels from one builder to another. Seeing someone pursue a vision with that level of commitment makes you want to raise your own standard too.
Uros is one of those builders.

description.content: A story about how a moment of pure panic ended up creating one of the most iconic symbols in digital design history.

content: In 2003, I was served a Cease and Desist notice by MTV Networks at my parents’ front door.
They claimed that my “[FWA][https://thefwa.com] ONE” award logo was too similar to their VH1 logo.
At the time, I was completely oblivious to the similarity. I was into raves, not watching MTV.
What followed was pure panic.
I spent the next 15 hours straight manually emailing 180 past winners, asking them to remove the award from their websites.
It was terrifying. Not only because of the legal threat itself, but because the whole situation exposed the fragile state of my mental health at the time.
But from those flames, something new appeared.

The team at CrashShop came up with the idea of sports-style ribbons. And from that idea came the iconic [FWA][https://thefwa.com] Yellow Ribbon: what would become one of the most successful “badges of honor” in web history.
It only exists because of that legal threat.
What began as a moment of fear and pressure became one of the most recognizable parts of the [FWA][https://thefwa.com] brand.

The ribbon has since been worn by thousands of websites, including 44 of the world’s top 100 brands. In 2011, the [FWA][https://thefwa.com] Yellow Ribbon even appeared on the homepage of an official LEGO Star Wars website.
Looking back, that moment proved something powerful:
friction often forces the best innovation.
We invited Rob because [FWA][https://thefwa.com] was one of the early sparks that helped us understand what digital could become.

For many of us, [FWA][https://thefwa.com] was never just an awards platform. It was a window into a different kind of internet: more expressive, more experimental, more emotional, and much more ambitious.
It shaped taste. It shaped standards. It shaped the way thousands of designers, developers, and studios looked at digital work.

For [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], especially from Argentina, platforms like [FWA][https://thefwa.com] opened a door to the world. They showed us that a website could be more than something functional. It could be an experience. A piece of culture. A place where design, technology, interaction, and emotion could come together.
Rob inspired us because he built one of those places. A platform that did not just recognize great work, but helped an entire industry look higher.

description.content: A reflection on being born digital, embracing change, and continuing to move forward even when the path is still being built.

content: Dave talks about the everyday decision that defines those who work in this industry: moving, adapting, looking for new ways to do things better, and accepting that, many times, building something meaningful means moving forward before having all the answers.
It is not an easy way to experience work. But when it works, there is nothing like it.
We invited Dave because there was a question he once asked that made us think differently.

It was not a question about a project, a scope, or a delivery. It was a question about the future, structure, and leadership. One of those questions that seems simple, but forces you to look at your own role from a completely different place.

Dave inspired us through that way of thinking: by looking beyond the immediate opportunity and understanding that growth is not only about getting more work, but about building an organization capable of sustaining a whole new level of ambition.

We were also inspired by his journey with [Metajive][https://www.metajive.com]: the clarity of its positioning, the standards he upheld, and the way he built with intention, vision, and long-term thinking.

Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], many people helped us look higher. Sometimes through a conversation. Sometimes through a question. Sometimes through a way of doing things that forces you to rethink your own.
Dave was one of those people.
My great-grandfather Julio, the father of my grandmother Mary, was born in Poland at the end of the 19th century. Six brothers and one sister, born into a proudly Jewish family.

European antisemitism and a severe economic crisis forced them to leave Europe. One ended up in Brazil, three in Australia, two in Israel, and he —Julio— arrived in Uruguay in 1928, leaving behind his wife Teresa and his son Abraham.

Although in Poland he had been a hatmaker, when he arrived in Uruguay, he did what so many others did: he went out selling door to door, house by house, field by field, around Paysandú, a small city in northwestern Uruguay.
The goal was very clear and concrete: to gather enough money to get his wife and son out of a country that did not want or respect them as quickly as possible.

How did they communicate? By letter? By telegram? How long did each exchange take? Did they send photos? Did they share news from the region? How did they miss each other? Did they write with hope? With humor? Were they afraid?
It was a different world.
9 years. Nine.

description.description: Julio, my great-grandfather, together with Teresa, my great-grandmother, who stayed in Poland with their son when he emigrated to Uruguay in 1928. Next to them is Abraham, the son who was born shortly before that departure, and in her arms is Mary, my grandmother, born already in Uruguay.

content: For nine years, my great-grandfather saved money for the passports and tickets. Without seeing them, without speaking to them. Until he finally made it.

And even though I try, I cannot imagine that reunion after nine years. At the port. A father looking for his son, who was no longer a child. A child who, without photos, possibly no longer remembered his father.
It seems insane to me.

Sometimes I get frustrated because the Wi-Fi is slower than I would like, or I get annoyed by the microwave beeping. Or I get angry at people speaking loudly on a bus or a plane and not letting me sleep peacefully.
Pure bullshit.
And then I try to gain perspective.
My great-grandfather spent nine years without seeing his family, working 14 hours a day, every day, and practically without communicating. I cannot get angry because the airplane food is horrible.
This story does not inspire me. It grounds me. It forces me to measure differently.
Inspiration lasts for moments —maybe minutes— and is possibly addictive. Like dopamine.
Sometimes we know where to look for it, and sometimes we do not.
Inspiration can appear unexpectedly in ordinary places: sunsets, showers, conversations, reels, books, walks. And many, many times, just as it appears, it disappears.

For a few minutes, it gives us the feeling of having found something magical. It makes us see beyond, imagine the future, the possibilities, the potential impact. It brings a little bit of the future into the present.
But with the same speed with which it appears, it disappears.
Inspiration is not constant, it is not a good advisor, and much less a good companion. It cannot be trusted.
That is why, when I try to think about the future, I do not look for inspiration, but perspective.
Because inspiration fades and disappears.
But perspective expands.
We invited Rafael because his conversations have always pushed us to think bigger.

From our first encounters, there was something about the way he looks at things that stayed with us: the ambition for scale, the search for impact, the ability to project forward and move a conversation out of its comfort zone into another level.

Rafael inspired us because he does not stay with the obvious. He has a way of challenging ideas, asking questions, and demanding depth that forces you to revisit your own standard. And many times, that is exactly what one needs in order to grow.

His story connects with that from another place: it does not speak about inspiration as something light or romantic, but about perspective. About looking at life, work, and everyday problems through a different scale. About understanding that some stories do not come to motivate you for a while, but to ground you forever.

Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we learned that there are people who inspire you because they make you step out of your comfort zone. People who force you to look further, think deeper, and measure differently.
Rafael is one of those people.
In 2011, I had a moment that completely changed the way I design.

I had just started at Akufen in Montreal. I had already been designing for a few years, but it was my first real role focused purely on web design. Honestly, I thought I was pretty good. My work looked solid, clients were happy, and I felt like I was doing exactly what I was supposed to do. I was cruising.

After my three-month probation, I had a meeting with the creative director to talk about what was next. I expected a normal conversation, maybe even a little praise. Instead, he told me something I still remember clearly: your work is good, but it doesn’t stand out.
He said he saw more potential in me, that I was capable of pushing much further, but I was playing it too safe.
It hit me hard.

I remember sitting alone in the hallway afterward, on a couch, just replaying the conversation in my head. I was frustrated, a little hurt, honestly a bit lost. I thought I was good. For the first time, someone I respected was telling me that good wasn’t enough.
That was the real click for me.
I decided my next project would be different. No more safe choices. No more doing just enough to make it work. I put everything into it. More time, more care, more obsession over details, more risk.
And it worked.

That project became my first awarded project, my first Site of the Day on [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com], something I had dreamed about for years. But the real reward was not the award. It was realizing that the difference between good and memorable is often just how much of yourself you’re willing to put into the work.

Since then, I’ve approached every project the same way. Big or small, exciting or boring, I always try to find that little extra thing that makes it matter. Sometimes all you need is someone to tell you the truth at the right moment. That tough love pushed me out of my comfort zone, and I still carry that lesson into every project I touch.
We invited Louis because his work has been a quiet but constant influence on the way we think about digital craft.

His approach to motion, interaction, rhythm, and detail helped shape how we look at the relationship between design and experience. Not just as something that should look good, but as something that should feel alive.
Over the years, through his work, talks, and courses, Louis has shared a way of thinking that pushes designers to care more, refine more, and go beyond the obvious solution.
His story makes that even clearer. It speaks about the moment when “good” stops being enough, and when someone’s honest feedback can push you to find the extra layer that makes the work memorable.
That is why Louis inspired us: because he reminds us that craft is not only about talent. It is about care, risk, obsession, and the willingness to keep pushing until the work truly stands out.

title: Three words that shaped a career

content: In 1970 I was a senior at Tyler School of Art, in Philadelphia, studying Illustration and Graphic Design. I had taken a Senior Graphic Design course and had Stanislaw Zagorski as my instructor.

"Mr. Zagorski", as we all called him, was a Polish illustrator who had designed and illustrated circus posters in Poland and had moved to the United States and designed and illustrated book and record covers. He did a cover for a rock band called “Cream,” who were a big deal then, and everyone in the class was super impressed. We hung on every word he said, which was hard because his English was terrible. We would show him our work and he would say, “Do over for me better.” He said it to everyone and if you argued with him, he would say it again. If he liked something he would hold it up to the class and say “good works” and nothing more. You had to figure out why it was good.

I had a hard time with typography in his class. Zagorski would assign book jackets and record covers as assignments. I would illustrate the covers, mostly with drawings or collages that related to the subject matter, but I never knew how to select or position the typography.

I didn’t relate to type at all. Most of the other students in class designed in the Swiss international style which usually amounted to 3 lines of Helvetica medium or bold in the upper left hand corner of the cover and they were done.

I hated the typeface Helvetica. I hated designing with it because I equated it with cleaning up my room. Also, I was pretty sloppy back then. We worked with press type which I could never lay down straight and it cracked and bubbled on my designs. I tearfully told Mr. Zagorski that I couldn’t design like the other designers in class.
He looked at me and said, “Illustrate with type.” In three words he had given me my whole career.
We invited Paula because, for us, she is simply one of the most influential people in the history of design.

Her work shaped the way generations of designers think about identity, typography, visual culture, and the role design can play in the world. She is one of those names that appears almost immediately when we talk about inspiration in our field.
And to be completely honest, we never thought she would answer.
We sent the invitation with admiration, respect, and a little bit of disbelief. But in less than 24 hours, Paula had replied, said yes, and shared her story with us.
That alone was incredibly meaningful.

For a studio like [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], celebrating 20 years from Argentina, having Paula as part of this project felt almost unreal. Not because of the name alone, but because of what that gesture represented: generosity, openness, and the idea that inspiration can move across generations, countries, and scales.
Paula inspired us long before this project existed. Through her work, her voice, her way of using type, and her ability to build a visual language that is unmistakably her own.
But her response also inspired us in another way: by reminding us that the people who shaped an entire industry can still answer with simplicity, speed, and generosity.
That is why having Paula in this archive means so much to us.

title: On the other side of the screen

description.content: Three stories about curiosity, decisions, and those moments that seem insignificant when they happen, but over time end up changing the course of a professional life.
Twenty minutes that shaped a path

content: In July 1995, I was backpacking through Europe with two friends. While passing through London, I had the chance to walk into a cybercafé, sit down, and try the experience. There were very few of them at the time.
After paying for a coffee, I went online for about 20 minutes. A Web accessed through a 28K dial-up connection, slow, and displayed in 256 shades of gray.

Although I was studying Social Communication, up until that moment I had not been entirely clear about what I wanted to do in the near future... It was after those 20 minutes that I told myself that, somehow, I had to work with whatever was on the other side of that screen.

description.content: Cannes, Cyber Lions and a new seed

content: Twenty years ago, I had a few fewer kilos, I was already wearing black T-shirts all the time, and while entering my sixth year at [Ogilvy][https://www.ogilvy.com], I received huge news: I had been invited to be a jury member at Cannes 2006 in the Cyber Lions category, as “digital” was called at the time.

It was an unforgettable experience: being able to share time, experiences, points of view, and opinions with professionals from all over the world, and being able to see work, projects, and campaigns from different markets, brands, and product categories.

That said, we never saw the beach, even though it was right in front of the Palais... Those were days of sitting in front of desktop computers at 8:30 in the morning and reviewing in detail between 250 and 300 entries per day, until we finished the lists assigned to each day.
The most enriching part came in the final phase, where we could discuss and debate the shortlisted pieces and which ones deserved metals.

Seeing the diversity and the range of executions that the “Cyber” category already covered at that time planted in me the seed of looking for other ways of doing things, an internal process that a year and a half later led to my move to [BBDO Argentina][https://www.bbdo.com.ar].

description.content: Lessons I still stand by

content: Well, the interesting thing is that I keep learning, if not every day, certainly every week. Lessons I can stand by? Let’s see...
It is relatively easy to be “creative” with enough access to resources; things get serious when it comes to being creative without those resources.
No amount of presentations or decks can replace work that has not been done: in our line of work, brilliant ideas that are not executed are, literally, useless.
A team is not a group of people who work together. A team is a group of people who trust one another.
You have to know the framework you are playing in, and what the rules are. Once you know the rules, you can break them or bend them.
There is no theory, someone else’s anecdote, data, TED talk, conference, or anything else that has the same value and impact when it comes to transferring knowledge as your own experience.
Never stop being curious, asking questions. You should never be afraid to search, investigate, ask, and want to find out more.
Related to the previous point: do not make assumptions before you start working. Working based on conjecture does not lead to many good places.

Sometimes you have to insist. If you truly believe that an idea is worth it, you have to insist. No one will be able to defend it the same way you or your team can. “The donkey doesn’t f*ck because it’s pretty, but because it insists,” as the popular saying goes.
Do not try to “fit in.” It is like Tetris: if you fit in by trying to belong, you stop being yourself, you disappear.
That’s it, and may [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] celebrate another 20 years! Onward! Congratulations!
We invited Fer because, for many years, he was an unavoidable reference for those of us trying to understand how far digital creativity could go.

His campaigns, his ideas, and his way of thinking pushed us not to settle for what was simply correct. To look for the uncomfortable, the unexpected, the thing that moves the needle. To understand that digital was not just a new format, but a territory where new ways of telling stories, interacting, and building experiences could emerge.

There were also concrete gestures that shaped our path. One of them was when he invited us to be featured on Fraser’s site. For us, it was one of those moments when you feel something click into place: someone you admired was looking at your work and opening a door.

Later came another important push: his support for us to join IADAS. Another gesture that may seem simple from the outside, but for us meant a lot in terms of validation, projection, and belonging to a bigger conversation.

Fer inspired us through his perspective, his curiosity, and his way of understanding creativity as something that refuses to settle. And also through that ability to open doors, push others forward, and raise the bar without making too much noise.

description.content: A reflection on teaching, trust, and that form of inspiration that appears when someone not only teaches skills, but helps keep the fire alive in those who are learning.

content: In this video, Marcelo returns to a deeply circular scene: 20 years ago, Lucas was his student at the University of Buenos Aires. Today, after four decades of uninterrupted academic activity, they share the same side of the desk as teachers.

Drawing from an idea in the book The Art of Blowing on Embers, Marcelo speaks about the role of a teacher as something that goes beyond teaching tools or skills. Teaching is also about detecting a glowing ember, caring for it, and helping it stay lit.
And within that perspective, something very simple and very powerful appears: it is not only about knowing how to do something. It is about trust, community, belief, and being good people.
A story about beginnings, education, relationships transformed by time, and the joy of seeing someone who was once learning on the other side now inspiring new generations as well.
We invited Marcelo because he was part of the true beginning of our path in design.

Before [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], before the studio, before the projects and the awards, there was a first class. A first presentation. A first time standing in front of teachers and classmates. And Marcelo was there.

His course was our first concrete contact with a deeper way of understanding design: with criteria, foundation, system, and language. A place where it was not enough for something to simply “look good”; you had to be able to think, explain, and stand behind your decisions.
That framework was foundational.

Over the years, the story took a beautiful turn: Lucas went from being Marcelo’s student to sharing the same academic space with him as a teacher. On the other side of the desk. In the same place where so many things had begun.

Marcelo inspired us because he represents one of the most important forms of inspiration: the inspiration that comes from those who teach. People who open minds, raise the bar, and leave a mark that we often only fully understand with time.
That is why we wanted him to be part of this archive. Because before building a point of view of our own, someone helped us learn how to see.

title: The Internet is Design in Motion

content: I was born in ’68. I have always been an illustrator, and I started designing when I was 18. I enrolled in university, but I did not even finish the first year because I realized I learned more by working. I learned in print shops, studios, and independent and network agencies, in a time when there were no computers and no Internet.

For many years, I was an Advertising Art Director, and that is where my creative background comes from. My training was in Creativity and Marketing. And I was always a freelancer, even when I was employed.

During my time in Advertising, inspiration could only come from thick, full-color annuals, which were very expensive and hard to find. The Book Fair was an opportunity to browse new annuals and beg the agency owner to buy one. Agency libraries were very modest, and sometimes colleagues who resigned or were fired would take one home.

When the Internet appeared, that whole paradigm changed. From my screen, I could find unlimited inspiration. And my work could also be seen all over the planet, not only when something was published in local newspapers or magazines.
Before the year 2000, I had already been exploring Web Design, but I barely knew how to make GIF banners. I would stay late at the agency learning HTML because I still did not have a PC at home.
And one day, inspiration arrived.

It was a short film made with Flash, an emerging technology at the time. An animation with background music that weighed only 350 Kb, created by Hillman Curtis, a now late designer and reference figure, who had a phrase that made me seriously consider moving into this new profession: “The Internet is Design in Motion.”

I wanted to make things with Flash, and I knew that in the job I had, inside an agency specialized in print and packaging, I would not be able to develop that. At the end of 2000, I left a good salary after almost 11 years and went home in search of web projects. I even had to buy a computer because I had always used the one at work.
I was 33 years old, the age of Christ. The advertising designer died, and the interactive designer was born.

In 2001, Argentina went through one of its darkest periods, with a major economic, social, and political crisis. Work was scarce, and very few people dared to “be on the Internet.” Until mid-2002, I lived alone, until I could not anymore and moved back into my parents’ house, who were already retired. I charged for the few jobs I did in patacones, a quasi-currency used during that crisis, but it worked for me because the supermarket accepted them.

In 2003, while we were all coming out of the crisis, and while splitting the cost of the Internet service with a neighbor, Digital Brand was born, my first personal portfolio. It was the manifestation of that inspiration I had received in 2000. That day, July 20, Friend’s Day, I launched my portfolio as a Flash Designer.

And from that point on, I never stopped working. As an employee or as a freelancer. Getting paid in australes, pesos, patacones, and dollars. I learned that whenever you work inspired, money eventually comes on its own.

Without looking for it, I became a national and regional reference. I worked for large and small brands and led both small and large work teams. In 2007, I resigned from a position as Creative Director at a digital agency to return to freelance work. Since then, I have continued working from home.

In 2009, I started working abroad thanks to Envato, the Australian platform for graphic and web design templates. And in 2014, I was able to stop working for the Argentine and Mexican markets and focus 100% on the American market. Today, I work as an Art Director at a digital agency in Long Island, New York.

My profession gave me many things, especially friends, many of them independent entrepreneurs like me. More than 20 years ago, I met Lucas Nikitczuk, today the leader of [studio NK][https://www.nk.studio], who invited me to write this testimony for his company’s anniversary. In his early days, while working in a position I had helped him get, Lucas was already beginning to shine on his own.

At one of the many end-of-year gatherings where I would run into Lucas, I told him: “When you work on your own, you’re going to do great.” And the rest is history. Just look at the portfolio and the many awards with which [studio NK][https://www.nk.studio] has been deservedly recognized over the past 20 years. A true Argentine pride with world-class quality.
An artist is a channeler of beauty or excellence. Ideas are not entirely ours: they appear, and our task is to give them shape. What we can choose is what things manage to ignite our inspiration.

In this initiative for [studio NK][https://www.nk.studio]’s 20th anniversary, you will find all kinds of triggers. Sources of inspiration of every kind. But do not expect to discover what inspires others in order to receive your own inspiration. That journey is personal.

Twenty years ago, I was employed at an agency but already thinking about going back to freelancing. Today I work from home, full-time remote. And at almost 60, I am still as inspired as I was that day.
In 20 years, you will be much further away than you are today. But never forget to take care of the energy that inspires you and to be grateful for it, so that flame remains abundant and permanent.
We invited Kaiser because, before [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] even existed, his work was already showing us that a website could be much more than a screen with information.

His sites had movement, rhythm, sound, interaction, and a visual sensitivity that, at the time, blew our minds. It was not just web design: it was experience, atmosphere, a new way of making something digital feel alive.

For many of us who started back then, Flash was a huge doorway. And Kaiser was one of those references who pushed that doorway a little further. Entering his sites meant looking, admiring, trying to understand how the hell it had been made, and feeling that there was a possible path there.
Our first Flash site was deeply inspired by that universe. By that mix of technique, beauty, exploration, and the desire to push the limits of what a website could be.

Over the years, that inspiration also became a bond. Kaiser was not only someone we looked at from afar, but someone who was close during the early stages, who saw something in Lucas even before [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] became what it is today, and who somehow also encouraged that path.

I discovered [/nk.studio][https://www.nk.studio] through [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com], while searching for production companies that paid great attention to detail and cared deeply about pixel-level quality.
When I found them, I felt very identified with their ambitious and entrepreneurial spirit. I couldn’t help but remember the time when I founded my own studio in Valencia, Pixelinglife.

Those were different times. Flash and ActionScript dominated the scene, but we fully shared the ambition to take the greatest possible care of quality in our interactive experiences. We couldn’t help feeling attracted to winning major industry awards, which back then meant [FWA][https://thefwa.com].
That is why, when I found [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], I saw them as continuers of that same spirit.

I chose them to work on several projects for one of our main and most beloved clients: [IKEA][https://www.ikea.com]. And on the first project, we achieved the most desired awards duo, what I call an FWAwwwards: [FWA][https://thefwa.com] and [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com], for [IKEA][https://www.ikea.com] “Red de Deseos.

Later, I had the chance to meet Lucas and his team both in Madrid and at the [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com] event in Valencia, in September 2024, and I was able to confirm that we shared a vision of the industry and that ambitious, entrepreneurial spirit that characterized Pixelinglife..
A spirit that today [/nk.studio][https://www.nk.studio] perfectly represents from Buenos Aires, Argentina, with the same desire to leave a mark on the industry.

We invited Miguel because, from the very beginning, he opened a huge door for us: the opportunity to work for a brand as meaningful as [IKEA][https://www.ikea.com], and to do so with an extremely high level of expectation.

His energy, attention to detail, and way of caring for every project deeply inspired us. With Miguel, it was never just about completing a delivery, but about pushing every experience to live up to the brand, the user, and the industry.

We were also inspired by his own journey. Pixelinglife represents a very special stage in interactive design: those years when Flash, ActionScript, [FWA][https://thefwa.com], and an obsession with quality shaped an entire generation of digital studios.

That is why it was so special for Miguel to see in [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] a continuation of that spirit. That ambition to care for every pixel, create memorable experiences, and leave a mark on the industry.

Over time, we shared projects, awards, and conversations that confirmed something very valuable: even when technologies, platforms, and eras change, there is a way of understanding the work that remains alive.
Miguel inspired us because he reminded us that standards do not belong to an era. They belong to the people who decide to uphold them.

description.content: If I have to think about something that truly inspires me, I often go back to Baricco. No a una frase puntual, sino a lo que me pasa cuando lo leo. Not to one specific quote, but to what happens to me when I read him.

content: In books like Silk, there is a way of telling a story where almost nothing happens… and yet everything happens. A glance, a minimal gesture, a silence. And you understand that there is something enormous there, even if it is not obvious.
And at some point, that started to make me question the way I was experiencing work.

Because we are very trained to think that value is in what is visible: in the results, in speed, in what can be shown. And Baricco, without saying it directly, moves you away from that. He forces you to slow down and look differently.
It changed me more than I expected.

It made me start paying attention to other things: to a difficult conversation someone dares to have, to a gesture of generosity under pressure, to someone holding the team together quietly, to those moments where “nothing happens”… but in reality, everything is being built.
Today, even in highly demanding contexts, I try not to lose sight of that.
Because in the end, work is not only what we deliver. It is what we generate along the way. It is the atmosphere, the trust, the way we treat each other when things do not go as planned.
And many of those things are not visible. But they are the things that remain.
Baricco reminds me of that.
That there is beauty —and responsibility— in the invisible.
And that perhaps leadership also has a bit of that: learning to see what is not obvious, and caring for it anyway.
Thank you for inviting me to return to this place.
We invited Patricia because her way of understanding leadership has inspired us for a long time.

There is one idea of hers that stayed with us deeply: when she stepped into a new role at [Globant][https://www.globant.com] and, instead of arriving by telling her team what had to be done, she asked them: “How can I help you?”

It may seem like a simple question, but to us it says a lot. It speaks of humility, listening, and a way of leading that does not stand above others, but in service of what the team needs in order to move forward.
Patricia inspired us through that way of showing up in the industry: with clarity, sensitivity, and a deeply human perspective on work.

description.content: A story about turning frustration into a global platform, making visible what used to be invisible, and building, together with the community, a new standard for the digital industry.

content: Before [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com], we were also a design studio.
Like many others, we wanted to create good projects, grow, compete, win opportunities, and find our place in an industry that was still taking shape.
At one point, we entered a selection process to try to win a project. But something about that experience did not feel right.
It was not just about being left out or not knowing whether we would win. It was something else.
The process felt opaque.

There was not enough clarity around the criteria. We did not really know why one project moved forward or why another one was eliminated. There was no feedback, no explanation, no response that helped us understand what had actually been evaluated.
And that lack of transparency left one question lingering:
What if there were a better way to recognize digital creative work?

A platform where the criteria were visible. Where you could know who was voting, what they were voting for, how they were voting, and under what principles. Where projects were not only showcased, but could also be evaluated, commented on, compared, and discovered by others.
We did not want to build a system designed only to charge the people submitting their work. We wanted to create a space that offered real value: visibility, criteria, transparency, and community.
That is how [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com] was born.
At the beginning, it was not “the global platform” many people know today. It was an idea driven by the belief that the industry needed something more open, clearer, and more participatory.
And from the very beginning, there was something fundamental: the community.
People who helped in a completely altruistic way. Designers, developers, studios, and professionals who believed in the idea, participated, voted, shared, and started shaping the system.
[Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com] did not grow only because a platform existed. It grew because there was a community that needed to meet, measure itself, get inspired, and recognize one another.
Over time, what was born from frustration became a meeting point for the global digital industry.

A place where thousands of studios discovered references. Where projects from anywhere in the world could gain visibility. Where design, technology, and creativity started to be observed through a higher standard.
[Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com] was born to make criteria visible.
But it ended up making something much bigger visible: an entire community of people trying to push digital work a little further.
We invited Dani because we cannot tell the story of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] without talking about [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com].

For us, [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com] was much more than a platform where we submitted projects. It was a window to the world. A benchmark. A standard. A mirror that made us look at ourselves and say: we can do better.

It pushed us to move beyond the local market, to measure ourselves against the best, to get inspired by other studios, to raise the bar, and to understand that digital design could be part of a global conversation.

Much of our growth is directly connected to the existence of [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com]. To that feeling that there is always someone, somewhere on the planet, doing something extraordinary.

title: Making do with what you have

description.content: A story about growing up in difficult contexts, learning to build without waiting for the perfect moment, and understanding that human conditions are also part of what makes any path possible.

content: A little over 20 years ago, I was 12. It was 2002 and, in the middle of Argentina’s crisis, my family went through a loss that changed us forever. So, at the beginning of my adolescence, I started to understand that there is no such thing as ideal conditions.

I grew up watching my mother make the impossible stretch, patacones included, keeping a home going with very little and moving forward anyway. I started working young, while I was still in high school, and later made decisions that did not seem like the most sensible ones: I studied art history with no money, no contacts, and no clear path. But to me, it made sense. If I had learned that even in the worst contexts there is always something you can do, then I could also build my own path with whatever I had at hand.

But I have another ace up my sleeve: along the way, I understood that it was not only about material conditions, but also about human ones. There was always someone who supported us/me, opened a door, gave me a hand, brought me an opportunity, and a thousand other things.

Sometimes they were people very close to me, and sometimes almost strangers. That also shaped me: knowing that the world helps much more than we usually believe or expect. And that one also has the responsibility to be available for others in the same way. Is it some kind of universal exchange? It doesn’t matter. I can testify that it works.

That idea still stays with me today. In my work, in projects, and in the way I approach problems, I first look at the conditions: what is there, what is missing, what limits, what enables. I build with those rules. Without romanticizing precariousness, but also without waiting for everything to be perfect in order to begin.

I suppose that, deep down, what I learned very early on is that a huge part of growing up consists of stopping asking why things were not given to you, and starting to see what can still be done, with what you have, and hand in hand with the people who are there and the ones who appear along the way.
We invited Bel because there are people who, even in a short amount of time, transmit a very clear energy.

In her, we saw drive, sensitivity, and a way of building that we find deeply inspiring. You can see it in her journey, in the culture she helped create, in the way she talks about projects, and above all, in that rare mix of ambition and humanity.

Bel inspires us because she pushes forward without becoming hardened. Because she creates space for others to grow. Because she understands that building something meaningful is not only about moving forward, but also about holding, opening doors, and being available for others.

Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we have learned that inspiration often appears in colleagues who are doing things with real conviction. People who are not only building companies, teams, or projects, but also ways of working and relating to others.
Bel is one of those people. That is why we wanted her to be part of this archive.

title: Daring to play in another league

description.content: A story about looking beyond the local market, turning adversity into momentum, and understanding that work also needs to be exposed, measured, and compared with the best in the world.

content: I was never aware, back in the inTacto days, that we could be an inspiration to others. It is really beautiful to hear that and to know that we were not just a passionate group chasing good design; knowing that we were able, even just a little, to positively influence the path of others is truly gratifying.
And honestly, I can say the same about you and NK. You are also an inspiration to me and to others; today, you are one of the strongest references in Argentina and the region.

We have known each other for years. We crossed paths at [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com] London 2015, we have worked on projects together, and at one point, pre-NK, you even had an interview at inTacto. Throughout all this time, I have been able to see your personal and professional growth, and the same with NK.

I think you have achieved something spectacular, reflected not only in the excellence and creativity of each project, but also in the team and the studio culture, which is one of the hardest things to build.
The initial spark, which would later become an unstoppable fire, happened during my time at FADU.

As a graphic design student, back in 1999, we used to buy the Communication Arts collection, the Behance of that time, haha. And I looked with admiration at those designers who managed to get their work published in that renowned collection.
My dream was to one day have a piece of my own work there.
Time passed, that vision grew stronger, and eventually that spark made big things take off.
Later, we founded inTacto Digital Partner, where we had two key moments that made us look beyond the local market.

The first one happened three months after we started, around December 2001, when the country had just exploded. We had not even managed to taxi down the runway and the runway had already been taken away from us. So we had no choice but to accelerate full speed and fly toward other markets, which opened many doors for us almost unintentionally.
That left us with a great lesson: sometimes adversity brings challenges that must be accepted in order to achieve positive things and grow even further.
The second key moment was also a difficult one that we managed to turn into something very positive, and it became our leap in quality and global exposure within the web industry.

It happened that, on the agency’s 10th anniversary, we had a significant drop in work and a large part of the team had free time. So we took advantage of that moment and created what became our first [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com]-winning project: inTacto 10 Years.

It is a very, very beautiful memory because everyone gave their very best with so much passion, and there was a very positive energy in the team, one of the most gratifying things that can happen when working together.
That was our beginning in the [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com] scene and the decisive moment that made us continue down that path.
More awards would come later, and then what became our top 1: Flat vs. Realism, the project that put us on the radar of major global agencies and changed the course of our story.

Looking back, many of our biggest leaps did not come from comfort, but from uncertainty. When the context became difficult, instead of stopping, we tried to use that time to create something that would push us to another level.

Twenty years ago, we were in a full growth stage at inTacto. And years later, a major professional turning point would arrive: MediaMonks, from the Netherlands, was looking to acquire an agency in Argentina. They wanted to combine talent with the New York time zone, and we were at our best moment.

We had been winning many international awards, the team was working at a very high level, and we began having many conversations with them, which ultimately led to the closing of the beautiful inTacto chapter.
Together with the whole team, we went on to open MediaMonks Buenos Aires.
Those were the global big leagues and, without a doubt, an unparalleled professional leap.
Years later, that same spirit would remain alive in new projects and new stages, as it does today with [Southmates Studio][https://www.southmates.com].

Our before and after came when we stopped working only for clients and started working for the industry and for ourselves too, deciding that our work not only had to function, but also had to be evaluated, criticized, and compared with the best in the world.
A good piece of work is useless if no one knows we exist.
Another key thing was paying attention to human relationships and teamwork: understanding and empathizing, leading and inspiring so that each person could join in and give their best.
Right there, in that precise moment, is where incredible things happen.

description.volanta: May the sparks keep lighting up
content: Finally, I want to congratulate you on this great project. The truth is that I never imagined that, in that attempt to surpass ourselves, we could also be inspiring others to dare to play that same game.

I have also been inspired by people both distant and close: my partner Sebastián, with his bold actions; the people on the team, with their different perspectives; and industry colleagues like you, whom I admire and with some of whom I now share great friendships.
They all form part of who we are and where we stand today; that is why I celebrate the fact that the sparks of inspiration continue to ignite and transform many more people with energy.
We invited Ale because, at a very early stage of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], he helped us understand that there was a much bigger world out there.

When we were still focused on doing the best work possible within the market we knew, seeing what Ale was building with inTacto became a signal. It was not just about designing well, but about daring to show the work, measure it, submit it, compete, and enter an international conversation.

For us, Ale was one of the first local references who truly pushed that standard. Someone who showed us that, from Argentina, it was also possible to play in the league of [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com], [FWA][https://thefwa.com], and the major global platforms.
Over the years, that inspiration became a real bond: encounters, conversations, projects, events, and a friendship built around a shared passion for design.

title: Calm is also a way of leading

description.content: A story about building teams with ambition and humanity, learning that balance also needs to be designed, and understanding that the relationships we care for can sustain even the most difficult moments.

content: I remember the time when I first became aware of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio].

Back then, every independent agency wanted to have a presence on platforms like CSS Design Awards, [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com], Dribbble, and Behance, among others. Their work already stood out on those platforms.

The projects we had at [Indicius][https://www.indicius.com] were quite varied at the time. The influence of Gizmo —and the fact that we shared offices with them— was what generated that diversity. We did websites and app design, yes, but also branding in general, branding for TV, and 2D/3D animation.
In a way, [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] fused all of that into the digital world at a time when technology was still limited.

[/nk][https://www.nk.studio] was always a reference when it came to unconventional projects in the digital world. They always stood out in that sense, they were always a source of inspiration, and I still believe there is no other studio in Argentina capable of achieving that level of quality for that kind of project.
It is an honor to be part of this project. Thank you for the invitation!
Twenty years ago,
I was just starting a “Web Studio” project, which six years later would become [Indicius][https://www.indicius.com].

I came from the corporate world, having worked at companies like IBM and Accenture, and I accepted an invitation from a friend to develop and lead the Web area of a multidisciplinary studio with three pillars: architecture, 3D animation, and web.
My friend used to create 2D plans and 3D animation for a partner in the USA, and that partner’s clients were asking for something new that everyone wanted at the time: websites.
That is how it all began.
One mission. Many lessons.

One of the things that resonated with me the most when I started leading a team was this idea —which became a mission— that it was possible to run a successful business without leaving the human side behind.
With ambition, yes, but measured ambition, and always putting people first.
I defended this idea fiercely with the owner of the company at the time, with clients, and with other members of the team who moved away from that premise.
This is one of the topics Lucas and I have always talked about, because we share that perspective, and because we always believed it was the right way to do things.
Were we successful? Of course we were.
Could we have been more successful? Definitely.

description.volanta: Balance is also something you learn
content: The biggest lesson is that everything requires balance.

It is not healthy to normalize your team working until any hour and/or during weekends, but it also does not help to overprotect them or make them believe that extra effort is a sin, especially when that dynamic is affecting the business.
The other big lesson is that the lack of that balance can be very costly, to the point of having to dismantle a beautiful team, as happened to us at [Indicius][https://www.indicius.com].
The positive side?
In most cases, all the good we gave came back in the form of empathy, understanding, and flexibility when going through that horrible process.
The relationships also remain, both professionally and personally, and that has immense value.
We invited Hernán because, at different stages of the journey, he showed us a very valuable way of standing in front of problems.

First, he was someone from the industry we looked up to. Then he became a client. And over time, he became a friend. But across all those versions, something remained constant: his calm, his professionalism, and his ability to bring perspective when the context became difficult.

Hernán inspired us because he never seemed to look at problems only from immediate reaction. Where there could have been tension, he brought serenity. Where there could have been noise, he helped create order. Where others saw conflict, he often found a broader, more strategic, and more human reading.
A story about uriosity, exploration, and the need to understand how things work in order to imagine, design, and build worlds that do not yet exist.

description.content: A story about curiosity, exploration, and the need to understand how things work in order to imagine, design, and build worlds that do not yet exist.

content: From a very young age, I had a connection with curiosity, you could say, with exploration, with understanding what made things work.

I always really enjoyed “building” things with different elements. A game that made an early click for me was building with Legos and Meccano, but I always understood them from a place of pure possibility, with their rules and physical limitations, as a framework set up for building.

I never liked or cared about following the manual for what to build with each set. Instead, in each of those boxes, I saw different key pieces that could help me build something I had in my head. When I saw a new piece in a toy store window, I understood that that piece enabled the possibility of building what I was thinking about, or of trying something I had not tried before.
That neural line is very marked in me. It unlocked something very early on, and from then on, I started thinking that way.
I always found it fascinating to invent universes and spaces with their own rules and forms. Acting as an orchestrator of those possibilities gave me enormous enthusiasm.

description.volanta: A black box full of worlds
content: Over time, that connected with my fascination for translating those physical worlds into what happened inside computers, starting with my first 286 with no hard drive, playing and designing in Banner, typing commands in DOS, where everything seemed possible, because somehow that black box made me feel that, maybe in an imaginary world, whatever I wrote there would allow me to do something different, searching through directories by typing /DIR, haha.

That beginning with computers kept deepening until I understood how systems worked, what made them move, what their general rules were. And with every update, even today, each incremental modification still impacts me as that space for exploring what is possible.

description.volanta: Understanding the rules in order to break them
content: From there came my deep dive into assembling and repairing computers, and even building what I believe was one of the first Hackintosh machines in Argentina, coding handmade drivers to make my video card work with a completely incompatible motherboard and a Pentium 4 — and making it work, and making it WORK WELL!

Those early computers came together, I think, with the golden age of PC games, also Sega, and with staring at every pixel, understanding how someone had thought it through, how every movement had been designed, from the intention behind it to why I found it brilliant.

That led to my curiosity to start designing myself the things I saw or used that had been designed by others. At that moment, I was not fully aware that they were simply —and not so simply— people who made those things exist and work.
The leap that didn’t happen
Exactly 20 years ago, I had a turning-point experience.

I was a self-taught Lucas, before starting university, but already with a sort of website business. I had around 10 clients with different websites, and on weekends I would ride my bike to collect maintenance payments. I applied for a position at what was then the emerging Fantasy.ai, previously known as Fantasy Interactive, because I admired their refined work in interfaces that, at the time, were completely mind-blowing, during the death and transition from Flash and ActionScript to HTML5.

With a humble but loving portfolio, they replied that they found my profile very interesting and gave me a challenge. But beyond the challenge, I was already pre-approved to move to Stockholm or New York, where they were just opening their US office, to become part of the team.
The challenge was to redesign the front page of an American newspaper, imagining what it would look like 10 years in the future.
All of that paralyzed me at the time, and I did not move forward on that path.

I do not know what would have happened if I had taken that leap of faith and moved to another continent, having barely traveled at that point in my life. But something pushed me more from a place of building something myself, whatever it took. And a few months later, an Alpha version of [DHNN][https://www.dhnn.com] was born.

DH, like NK, is close to turning 20 and has gone through all kinds of nuclear transformations. If I am not wrong, there have already been four of them. And each one implies a reset, but with a lot of previous knowledge.

A continuous act of exploring, opening paths, taking risks, and believing in how to transform the world through the discipline that moves me: designing and making things that do not yet exist, exist, work, and contribute to the world, like an engine that turns ideas into something concrete.
The engine is still on

In the same way, I found a parallel in mountaineering: in exploring, leaving the path, facing the difficulties before reaching the goal, and everything that happens along the way. Going through the process, learning to enjoy it, and realizing that even if you finish a journey completely exhausted or even injured, you do not hesitate to do it again.
Because that engine is still on.
Ready for one more.
We invited Lucas because, for years, [DHNN][https://www.dhnn.com] was an unavoidable reference for those of us building our own path in the digital industry.

Before we met, before we worked together, and before there was any close relationship, there was already admiration. DH represented a standard: a way of designing, of presenting itself, of sustaining criteria, and of building its own identity within the market.

For [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], looking at what DH was doing meant looking at a high bar. A sign that from Argentina it was also possible to build with ambition, quality, and a clear point of view on what a creative company could be.

Over time, that inspiration became a bond. We started crossing paths, sharing conversations, projects, and stages. And something that at first had been a silent reference began to transform into a relationship between peers, with mutual respect and shared learning.

Lucas inspired us because he built things his own way. Because he sustained a vision over the years, went through transformations, reinvented himself more than once, and kept exploring without losing that initial impulse to make things exist.
That is why we wanted him to be part of this archive. Because there are colleagues who, without knowing it, set a standard for you. And over time, those references become part of the journey.
A story about how a personal loss can trigger a profound change, and how sharing knowledge without expecting anything in return can become a way to help, grow, and build community.

In this video, Alan talks about his journey as a content creator, programmer, and educator. He shares how [Gentleman Programming][https://www.youtube.com/@GentlemanProgramming] was born during the pandemic, from a simple but powerful question: how can I help people?
What started as an altruistic initiative became a real community. People who learned, found jobs, improved their situation, or found in his content a guide to keep moving forward.

Alan also shows the other side of that path: the effort, the sacrifices, the hours after work, family, open source, guides, videos, and the consistency required to sustain something that is not always visible from the outside.
A story about generosity, community, and the power of sharing what you know.
We invited Alan because we deeply admire the way he shares knowledge.

Not only for what he knows, but for how he puts it at the service of others. For the energy he dedicates to explaining, teaching, organizing complex concepts, and making programming more accessible to those who are learning.

Alan inspires us because he understands that knowledge does not become more valuable when it is kept, but when it circulates. When it helps someone get a job, improve, take a step forward, or simply feel accompanied on a path that can often be difficult.
Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we learned that inspiration often appears in people who do what they love with enormous generosity.
Alan is one of those people. Because he shares, teaches, and builds community without losing his passion for the craft or the humanity behind the code.
The impulse to materialize an idea

What inspired me to found Primate was mainly one of my lifelong dreams: to create and manifest something real. To transmute creativity and imagination into something tangible in this world. That relationship between thinking and then creating, between conceiving an idea and materializing it, always fascinated me, and I had never had the opportunity to put it to the test.

After a very successful year, full of deep and revealing changes, I decided to put that dream to the test. That was when I set out to start and lead a project of my own. With the resources I had managed to obtain through my profession, I felt I had nothing to lose and that it was the right time to try.

The industry I chose was gaming, specifically the Esports niche in Argentina. I had always been passionate about games since I was a kid, and that year, 2021, competitive gaming was booming internationally, mainly in Europe and the United States. Like most things, none of this had really arrived here yet: there was a developing scene, but still on a small scale. That had everything that attracts me: a taste of challenge, opportunity, and above all, risk.

Risk is something that has always pushed me a lot, and I am usually prone to seek it out and take it. I can say that this search for risk, and being willing to look and go where others perhaps do not even consider, is one of the main factors that has given me so much in life.
The closing as a turning point

I believe that, in the particular case of the Primate process, if there is one moment to highlight as a turning point, it is clearly the decision to close it. After three years of trying, tooth and nail, constantly pushing forward against all odds and within an industry in constant decline, due to the nature of the market, the moment I finally decided to put an end to the project marked a huge before and after in my life.

It completely transformed not only my life, but also my way of seeing the world, my relationships with others, and my relationship with myself. It was one of the most delicate moments of my life, almost like watching a child die, because for me that is what it was, and I experienced both its birth and its eventual death.
It may sound drastic to put it in these words, and the truth is that during the process it was very hard. But I want to make it clear because the change it brought to my life was profoundly positive.
There are countless things I could mention that I learned during that grief, but if I can briefly mention a few, they are mainly:
Courage/Bravery: Having the courage and strength to end something that had eventually completed its cycle.
Determination, Resilience, and Trust: Accepting the nature of life. Everything that is born eventually dies, the cycle of life. And everything is born again too.
Learning to let go and to heal. Understanding and surrendering to processes. Accepting what is.
Neutrality toward results and focus on processes.
Getting to know oneself deeply through adversity and challenges.

Integrity: What one is, in every sense and form, is transferred to what one creates and manifests. As within, so without. Who one surrounds oneself with, what one thinks, is what one does and consequently what one says. This is one of the most important things to pay attention to, in order to enjoy the journey and not lose perspective on progress and the path.

Entrepreneurship was one of the most challenging and exciting stages of my life. It took me completely out of my comfort zone and stretched me to unknown limits. It helped me gain perspective and become a better person.

description.volanta: Trying again with a different perspective
content: My way of seeing the world and my short but deep experience at 30.
If I were to try again, these are the things I would do differently. Today, I would not change anything, because thanks to everything I did, I received the vision and experience I now have.

Desire and Passion: This is the most important thing of all. There must be an engine fed by infinite fuel to face challenges day after day. The desire must be burning and passionate; it is the only way to truly give everything and move forward. But it is also the way to fail forward and iterate.
If there is an intrinsic desire that cannot be extinguished and cannot be defeated, genuine from the heart, mistakes and challenges are simply lessons to try again, but better.

Less fear of failing: Fail-fast and fail-safe is something to apply constantly. It allows you to pivot and learn much faster. If one is 100% committed, mistakes will show us the way that is not right, and the way that actually is.

+Isolation +Confidence +Determination: Something I would definitely do differently is spend and have excessively more time alone.
