In an organization, one is constantly tied to decisions that involve others, structures, bureaucracy, discussions, and most decisions require a back-and-forth, whether with partners, the board, etc.

The reality is that the vision and soul of the project are born and live within the founder’s plane of ideas. That is why, if there is something I would change, it would be to pay much more attention to the creative processes and ideas, and act on them once they have been analyzed and internally tested.

The founder is the one with the most skin in the game. And is the person who best understands what is being created. That is why all the “isolated” time chewing on and processing ideas, I believe, leads to much more confidence and determination, less noise, when communicating and implementing them with teams and partners, and defending the position and vision with determination when necessary.

Balance and Processes over results. It took me years and fortunes to understand this concept. An excessive focus on results creates toxic and destructive environments. On the contrary, focusing on healthy and gradual processes allows everything to flow with less resistance, converging into results that arrive as the effect of a clear and consistent process.
The end.
We invited Ramón because he was the person who opened the door to a completely new world for [/nk][https://www.nk.studio]: the universe of eSports.

Primate was not simply our first project in that industry. It was an experience that forced us to understand another way of building a brand: through community, competition, belonging, spectacle, and culture.

Ramón inspired us through the passion with which he spoke about what he was creating. It was not just about building a team, but about building an identity. A home. A vision. Something that could represent a community and project itself into the future.

We were also inspired by the way he went through the process: with risk, conviction, intensity, and enormous honesty in seeing both the birth and the closing of Primate as parts of the same learning experience.

There is something deeply valuable in those who dare to create, but also in those who have the courage to let go when a cycle has been completed. Ramón reminded us that entrepreneurship is not only about starting something. It is also about learning how to read processes, sustain a vision, accept endings, and be transformed by them.
Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], many people inspired us by opening new paths. Ramón was one of them.

I started [Zetenta][https://zetenta.com] 22 years ago while I was studying, and getting frustrated with, Computer Engineering at the University of Buenos Aires. I was building HTMLs, without CSS or JS, in Dreamweaver, and creating applications in Visual Basic. Over time, things started to grow until I left university, focused fully on work, and created the agency.

I was always very organized, detail-oriented, informed about technologies, and full of good intentions. But there was something that was incredibly hard for me during the first 10 years: developing my soft skills, or human skills, in order to become a good leader. My engineering-oriented and structured profile did not help at all. I hit many walls because of my limitations, and I learned lessons along the way.
At one point, a very dear developer who was leaving the agency after several years left me a book as a farewell gift: The Servant by James C. Hunter.
That book marked me. It proposes that leading well is not about imposing authority, but about building it through empathy, discipline, consistency, generosity, and human values.
For me, it was a turning point: the seed that made me understand that human skills were not something accessory, but an essential foundation for leading well and building a good work culture.
To this day, I continue working on those values and those skills.

And today, more than ever, I am convinced of their importance. In a world shaped by artificial intelligence, technical skills are becoming increasingly accessible and automatable. What makes the difference are human skills: sensitivity, judgment, empathy, communication, curiosity, and the ability to inspire, among others.
Building teams with strong human values is not only still important: it is probably more important than ever.
We invited Lucas because he was part of a very important stage in our professional journey, a stage where we learned that detail, judgment, and standards were non-negotiable.

At [Zetenta][https://zetenta.com], we saw a way of working defined by care, organization, and a healthy obsession with doing things well. Not “more or less.” Not “good enough.” Well. With intention, method, and respect for the work.
Lucas inspired us because he showed us that detail is not a whim: it is culture. That craft matters. That sustaining a standard is also a way of leading.
Over time, that experience became even more meaningful. Before defining our own standards, we learned them. Before building a culture, we saw how others sustained one in the everyday work.

And his story adds another very valuable layer: that of someone who, coming from a technical and structured background, understood that leading well requires more than knowledge. It requires empathy, communication, sensitivity, consistency, and human values.

That is why we wanted Lucas to be part of this archive. Because much of what [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] is today also has seeds planted in that stage: in the detail, in the method, in the commitment, and in the constant pursuit of doing things better.
When I started working at an artificial intelligence consultancy, I spent several months without finding my place.
I come from communication, marketing, and user experience. Suddenly, I found myself listening to acronyms and concepts I had no idea how to understand.
All of this was years before ChatGPT existed, so I had no one to quickly ask. There was no manual, no context, and no kind answer waiting on the other side of a chat.

The breakthrough came when I started having one-on-one conversations with my engineer and data scientist colleagues. When they told me, in their own words, how what they did changed other people’s everyday lives.
People telling little stories.

That is what it ends up being. Not the spotlight on whoever knows the most about technology, but on those who know how to translate, connect, and make the complex land in a way that someone else can hold.
There was no need to know how to code. No need for a PhD. What was needed was a critical perspective and the desire to enter the conversation.

Mass artificial intelligence did not only automate tasks: it opened the field. Natural language became the interface. Participating no longer requires knowing so much code; more than ever, it requires thinking, asking, reading contexts, and understanding people.
The technical barrier that kept many people out for years has come down. And yet, the conversation is still in the hands of a few, because having access is not the same as daring to use it.

Today, a much bigger conversation is developing than whether the code should be this way or that way: it is about how we are working, what we are going to delegate, how we are going to relate to one another, and what foundations are shaping a new world.
And that conversation needs people who know how to read people, organizations, and moments. People who can see what others cannot see because they are standing too close to the focus.
People who know how to tell little stories.
We invited Lucia because her way of elevating conversations has always inspired us, even in complex contexts.
Beyond professional cycles, there was something we always deeply valued: her clarity, her judgment, and her ability to handle difficult situations with balance, respect, and humanity.
Lucia inspired us because she understands that leading is, in part, about translating, organizing, and holding conversations where others might get stuck in tension or complexity.

Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we learned that inspiration often appears in people who not only know how to do, but also know how to explain, open conversations, and help others better understand what is in front of them.
Lucia is one of those people.

title: The inspiration that comes from friction

description.content: A story about discovering a path without having certainty, turning someone else’s doubt into your own momentum, and understanding that sometimes inspiration does not come to tell you that you can, but to ask you how willing you are to try anyway.

content: My first contact with design did not come from a clear vocation, nor from that romantic kind of inspiration where someone discovers exactly what they want to do with their life.
It came more from an internal discomfort, a need to move toward somewhere else, even if I still did not know exactly where that was.
At the company where I worked, the designer had been let go and a lot of pieces were left unfinished: flyers, newsletters, ads for media outlets, and social media posts.

It was the early years of the digital boom, when the idea was beginning to take hold that if a brand was not on the internet, did not have a presence on social media, or did not have a website with a good user experience and a modern interface, it was practically left out.

At that moment, I already felt that I wanted to change roles, to do something different from what I had been doing. And even though I had no design training, I offered to take that place. More out of impulse than certainty.

I started by solving whatever I could. Learning Photoshop and Illustrator along the way, literally while I was making the pieces. Everything was quite intuitive, trial and error. But there was something in that process that deeply captivated me.
I liked the idea of building something visual, communicating, giving shape to an idea.
But above all, I was fascinated by that moment when an idea stopped existing only in your head and started coming to life in front of someone else’s eyes.
How something that, just a few hours earlier, did not exist could become a piece capable of communicating, generating a reaction, or even becoming a useful tool for someone else.
Information that another person received in order to decide, understand, become interested, or do something with it.
There was something very powerful in that. In the possibility of turning abstract thoughts into something tangible, visible, and shared.
It was in that context that I met the person who was developing the company’s new website. I was on the client side, leading the project, and he was the provider in charge of design and development.
So I started asking him everything.
What day-to-day work was like, how they organized projects, what tools they used, how they made decisions, what it was like to work with clients, how creative processes worked.
Even things that seem normal today, like working from a coworking space, were completely new to me at the time.
More than revealing, all of it felt deeply interesting. It was discovering a world that, until then, I had not known existed in that way.
And all that information, every conversation, enriched me enormously.
In one of those conversations, I told him that I wanted to go deeper into the world of design, specifically digital design: website design, digital experiences, digital branding.

I felt the need to give a theoretical framework and more context to everything I had already been doing intuitively. Because until then, much of my learning had been self-taught, built through curiosity and everything I could find online.
And then came a phrase that I never forgot, and that also triggered many emotions in me.
He said something like:
“I would look for another branch within the industry… maybe something more oriented toward community management. To start with design, maybe you are a bit late.”
At that moment, I was 23 or 24 years old.

And although he probably did not say it with bad intentions, that phrase stayed with me. Over time, I understood that it probably came more from a place of protection and from a mindset that was quite common at the time: the idea that what you studied almost permanently defined your professional path.
But I never worked that way. Not before, and not after.

And far from stopping me, that phrase created exactly the opposite effect. It awakened a very deep need in me to do it. Without too many doubts. As if something inside me had been activated in that instant and there was no turning back.
The strangest thing of all is that, for a moment, I believed him.

Because when someone who is already inside a world tells you that maybe you arrived too late, something inevitably moves. Especially when you are still trying to understand whether you really belong there.
But I think that was precisely when something important appeared.
Not certainty. Not validation. Not even confidence.
A need appeared.
The need to try anyway.
Over time, I understood that inspiration often works like that.

It does not always come from someone who pushes you forward or tells you “you can do it.” Sometimes it comes from friction. From something uncomfortable. From an external resistance that, unintentionally, ends up revealing how much you truly want something.
Over time, I understood that that conversation was one of those moments that change a direction without announcing it.

And a change of direction never only means moving from point A to point B. It also touches something much deeper: your own belief system. What we think we can or cannot do. What we believe is right, possible, logical, or expected.
I also understood something else: that inspiration does not always appear in the most obvious ways.
We often think of inspiration through admiration, through someone we idolize, through a motivational talk, a reference, or a success story. And of course, that kind of inspiration exists.
But there is another kind, perhaps quieter and more powerful.
The inspiration that comes from friction.
From someone who doubts. From someone else’s limit. From a refusal that, unintentionally, ends up awakening your own certainty.

Because sometimes inspiration does not appear to give you answers. Sometimes it appears to force you to discover how willing you are to sustain what you feel, even when someone else still cannot see it.
Sometimes inspiration does not come to tell you that you can.
Sometimes it comes to ask you how willing you are to do it anyway.
With Emi, we shared a foundational stage. A stage of searching, disagreements, decisions, learning, and growth. The kind of stage that is not always simple, but ends up leaving real marks.
And there is one gesture in particular that is still alive today: the slash.

That symbol, which now defines our name and our identity, was born from his reading of something as simple as the way we wrote our emails, and finding a signal there. A small observation that ended up becoming a huge part of who we are.
Emi inspired us because he helped us see ourselves differently.

Because often, the people who mark us the most are not only those who accompany us through the easy moments, but also those who push us to think better, to discuss things more deeply, and to build with more intention.
That is why we wanted him to be part of this archive. Because there are people who do not just pass through a story: they become part of it.
Not every path has a before and after; some are built in between.
For a long time, I thought my story was missing something: that clear moment that organizes everything, that turning point that explains the path.

Over time, I realized that what I did have was a constant process of deconstruction. An exercise in reviewing assumptions, questioning decisions, and letting go of what no longer makes sense. Not as a reaction, but as a way of operating.

Looking back, there was already an impulse present since I was a child. At home, I learned from my parents the value of work and effort; not to stay still, to move forward, to pull in the same direction even when it was not easy. At 16, a dance teacher saw something in me that I still could not see: the ability to lead. I became a certified aerobics instructor — between anatomy and physiology books — and I was already teaching classes. I put together a group of 25 girls and we competed against schools with more experience. We ended up champions, fun fact :)
That is when something settled in me that still accompanies me today: to trust, to push, and to go for more.

At 18, I moved out on my own, from Bariloche to Mar del Plata. I chose a degree more out of obligation than vocation, and still finished it. Not because it was perfect, but because moving forward does not always come with certainty.

Some time later came the part no one teaches you. Moments when life is not easy: it is hard. When it breaks any predictable narrative and confronts you with scenarios you did not choose. There is no immediate lesson, no meaning. You simply have to be there, hold on, keep going. Not because you want to, but because there is no alternative.

And that is where any speech ends. You do not move forward because you want to. You do not move forward because you are motivated. You move forward because there is no other option. That is when something different appears. A form of strength that is neither epic nor inspiring. It is concrete, silent, necessary.

That way of moving through the personal inevitably carries over into the professional. I have been working in the tech industry for more than 12 years, where I had the opportunity to learn from people who raised my standard. But I also understood that what truly defines growth is not only the environment, but the individual ability to question it.

Curiosity, judgment, and autonomy cannot be delegated; they must be practiced. Not every environment empowers, not every leadership cares. And recognizing that is part of building a career with intention. That is when I fully assumed something central: no one is going to protect your well-being if you do not do it yourself.
That idea not only organizes decisions, it also defines standards: where to be, what to build, what to sustain, and what to let go of.

My story does not have one clear turning point. It has decisions, moments that force you to change, and the right people by your side to sustain that process. I did not always choose what happened to me, but I did choose how to stand in front of it. And, over time, that ended up defining everything else.
We invited Nati because she represents a way of doing things that we deeply admire: the kind of person who pushes every day to make things happen.
Nati inspires us through her energy, her consistency, and her ability to move conversations forward, connect people, organize processes, and sustain progress even when the context is not simple.

There is something very valuable in the way she shows up: she does not wait for everything to be perfect before taking action. She brings people together, follows up, insists, cares, and pushes. And many times, that kind of energy is what turns an idea into real movement.

Her story shows something we also see in her work: a concrete, silent, and deeply human strength. Not the epic strength of big speeches, but the strength of someone who learned to move forward even when there were not many certainties.
Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we learned that inspiration often appears in people who sustain, connect, and help others move forward too.
Nati is one of those people.

description.content: A reflection on leadership, clarity, and the ability to hold difficult conversations when the context is constantly changing.

content: Gini Lustig COO & Partner, [Indicius][https://www.indicius.com] Buenos Aires, Argentina
In this video, Gini revisits a project she shared with [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] and an idea that stayed with her: taking the floor.

But not from the place of having everything solved or under control. Because in intense projects, with changing clients, many rounds of back and forth, and decisions constantly in motion, absolute control does not exist.

For Gini, taking the floor has more to do with something else: being able to say yes to this, no to that. Having the courage to hold uncomfortable but necessary conversations. Helping set boundaries, organize uncertainty, and create clarity collaboratively.
A form of leadership that is not based on having all the answers, but on knowing how to read the context, hold the conversation, and help the team move forward.
We invited Gini because, at an important stage of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], she helped us understand something that goes far beyond language: what it means to take the floor.
In a project we worked on together, she held many of the most important conversations. She listened, interpreted, organized, and transformed ideas into clear, confident, and precise messages.

Gini inspired us because she showed that leading a conversation is not simply about speaking. It is about representing, translating context, setting boundaries when needed, and helping others move forward with more clarity.

And, personally, she also left a very concrete mark: she pushed us to grow, to prepare ourselves better, and to understand that to play in certain scenarios, we had to be ready to take the floor with more autonomy.

title: Stepping out of the comfort zone without losing who you are

description.content: At [Veritran][https://www.veritran.com], for years we moved naturally within the world of technology for the financial industry. It was our territory, our language, our comfort zone. Until an opportunity appeared that forced us to look beyond: becoming an Official Global Partner of Manchester City and, from there, starting to build a new way of connecting.

description.volanta: The story of a great partnership
content: It was not just about a partnership. It was about entering the world of football, with everything that implies: passion, emotion, history, identity, and culture. A completely new territory for a B2B company like ours.

The challenge was not technical. It was conceptual. Because it was not about stopping being who we were, but about bringing our essence into a completely different context. Continuing to speak to a B2B audience, while incorporating a closer, more emotional dimension, one more connected to the B2C world, capable of elevating the brand without losing depth.
That is where the real question appeared: how do you connect two worlds that, on the surface, do not seem to have much in common?

The answer was not to change, but to translate. To understand that, deep down, both universes share something essential: people. And that even in the most complex businesses, decisions are also moved by connection, experience, and emotion.

Along the way, the support of [studio nk][https://www.nk.studio] was key. Together with their team, we found a way to turn this vision into action, combining strategy, creativity, and execution in record time.

In a matter of weeks, we found ourselves producing, all at once, a launch event, social media content, a website, audiovisual pieces for events, animated billboards for the Etihad Stadium, and even a themed photo opportunity that allowed us to bring that experience into the physical world. All under extremely high quality standards, both from the club and from our side.
There was pressure. There were stressful moments. But there was also something stronger: the conviction that we wanted to rise to the occasion. And we did.
Throughout that process, the work with [studio nk][https://www.nk.studio] was decisive in sustaining the pace, elevating the quality, and bringing every piece to the level the project demanded.

That process transformed us. Not because we changed who we were, but because we expanded the way we expressed it. We incorporated a new layer into our communication without losing the core: the same solidity, the same logic, now crossed by a narrative capable of connecting from a different place.

The impact was immediate. Internally, it generated pride. Externally, it opened new conversations. It allowed us to be on the field, at events, in direct contact with clients and potential clients from a completely different place.
But above all, it left us with one certainty: stepping out of the comfort zone is not just a strategy. It is a decision that redefines what you believe you are capable of doing.

Today we know we are ready for any challenge we set for ourselves. And that when conviction, creativity, and courage combine with the support of the right partners, even a B2B company can find new ways to connect without losing who it is.

description.volanta: Why Flor and Gina inspired us
content: Because they represent a way of working that we deeply admire: the kind of people who uphold a high standard every day, even in the details not everyone sees.

In every project we shared, we saw commitment, judgment, and a huge sense of responsibility for caring for the brand. Not from the specific request, the deadline, or the urgency, but from something much bigger: understanding that every piece is part of a story, an experience, and a way of connecting with people.

Flor and Gina inspired us because they uphold the standard with a conviction that is not common. In high-pressure contexts, where everything has to be done well and fast, that way of showing up makes an enormous difference.

Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we learned that inspiration also appears in the everyday: in the people who care for every detail, elevate every delivery, and trust enough to build something bigger together.
Flor and Gina are part of that kind of inspiration.

description.content: A story about carrying forward a family legacy, professionalizing a company with history, and understanding that growth also means taking care of the people who make that journey possible.

content: First of all, thank you for thinking of us and for your words. This project you are building is amazing. It is really beautiful to see companies led by people we care about, colleagues and friends, grow, evolve, and stand the test of time, especially in a country as complex as ours. So congratulations on these 20 years.
In [Tecnon][https://www.tecnongroup.com/]’s case, one of the turning points was when we started looking inward, with a conscious decision to improve and professionalize the company.
For many years, we grew mainly supported by the technical quality and strong reputation our brand had always had in the market.
But in recent years, we took a more intentional step: organizing processes, investing in technology, strengthening management, and working on communication.
That shift in mindset made a difference in the way we think about the company.
Being the third generation of the family means, for me, an important commitment and pressure, but in a beautiful way.
It also means maintaining a permanent balance between respect and evolution.

There is a very solid foundation built on craft, seriousness, and long-term relationships with clients, suppliers, and colleagues in the industry. That intangible capital is enormous, and we take great care of it.

At the same time, we understand that honoring that legacy does not mean preserving everything exactly as it is. It means daring to question what is no longer enough, professionalizing management, and preparing the company for what comes next.
In that sense, evolving without losing identity is a beautiful challenge.
Perhaps the most important lesson for me has to do with the human dimension of the company.
In a family-owned SME, you quickly understand that behind every process there are people, and behind every person there is a family.

Growing sustainably is not only about improving indicators or numbers. It is also about taking care of people, respecting their journeys, creating opportunities for development, and sustaining relationships of trust over time.
Technology, processes, and strategy are essential, but without a culture of genuine respect for people, growth cannot be sustained.
And that growth requires intention, method, and a lot of commitment.

content: Lastly, a special mention to the companies and people we have worked with throughout the different stages of the company’s history.
Those who become strategic partners and even friends. People and teams you are truly grateful to have crossed paths with along the way.
And clearly, [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] and its entire team are one of them.

I always say that working with you was a pleasure for us. From the very first meeting, I felt and saw a genuine intention to understand who we are as a company and as a family, and that is not something we always find.
Thank you again for the invitation to be part of such a beautiful initiative, and congratulations on the anniversary.
Here’s to many more years of beautiful projects.

In her, we see a very valuable perspective: respect for what has been built, but also the determination to professionalize, organize, communicate better, and prepare the company for what comes next.

In Argentina, that has enormous value. Sustaining a family business is already a challenge. Growing it, transforming it, and projecting it into the future without losing its identity requires sensitivity, conviction, and a lot of commitment.

Bianca inspires us because she understands that a company is not built only through processes, technology, or strategy. It is also built through people, relationships, trust, and a culture that is cared for every day.

title: From seeing the impossible to becoming part of it

content: When I was 18, I was working at a small studio in Mar del Plata.

One day, the owner showed me [Awwwards][https://www.awwwards.com] and said: “This is the best of the best in web.” I went in, started browsing, and it blew my mind. On one of those pages, I reached the footer and saw that the studio was from Buenos Aires.
I couldn’t believe that something like that existed so close by.

I started following them on Facebook and Instagram, and a few days later Lucas added me and wrote to me because he had seen what I was posting. He offered me the chance to do a freelance project together.
For me, that alone was already huge.

But the moment that really marked me was when he sent me the design. I was leaving my house to go to university, saw the email, stopped, opened my computer, and when I saw what was there… I couldn’t believe it.
I was completely in shock.
I told my mom: “This is Europe-level,” even though she didn’t really understand what I was talking about.
I did that project as the happiest person in the world. And when I delivered it, Lucas said to me: “IM PE CA BLE. You know I’m detail-oriented, but I have nothing to say.”
That’s where everything started.
Today, we’ve been working together for almost 12 years, and everything we’ve built at [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] is, without a doubt, the most inspiring thing that ever happened to me.
What marked me the most was realizing that something I saw as extremely far away, almost impossible, was actually right there. And that someone was trusting me to do it.
It was like a click in my head.
It made me understand that I could be at that level. That it wasn’t something reserved for others. And it also taught me the importance of betting on someone.
That first push changed everything.
From that moment on, I never saw my work the same way again.

description.content: A story about first teams, first corrections, and the people who, without knowing it, help shape the standard with which others will later build.

content: In 2007, WebAr invited me, together with a colleague, to lead a smaller agency.
That was where we first heard about Lucas, through Matías, someone we had hired shortly before. We were looking for another semi-senior designer, so we interviewed him right away.
It took us a while to move forward with his hiring because we had several CVs on the table. But Lucas insisted almost daily. He would write to ask whether we had already made a decision.
Persistent, yes.
But he also showed interest.
And that was a plus.
From the beginning, what caught our attention was how well he worked, how fast he was, and how willing he was to learn new things related to design.
Back then, HTML was built with divs and CSS. If I remember correctly, Lucas learned by researching, testing, and correcting under our supervision.
It was not just talent.
It was a way of approaching the work.
Looking, testing, receiving feedback, adjusting, and then applying that learning again in the next project.

Over the years, you understand how much those things matter. Because at an early stage, it is not always about knowing everything, but about having the right attitude to learn, improve, and build judgment.
Another thing I remember very clearly was how passionate he was about design.
Lucas never delivered work that lacked quality. I have met very few people like that over the years.
He did not only dedicate time and care to design. He also researched and was open to the corrections that came up in his work.
The good thing was that he applied those same correction criteria to future projects.
And to me, that is an important sign.

Because a standard does not appear overnight. It is formed through everyday work. Through projects. Through corrections. Through uncomfortable conversations. Through learning that doing things well is not only a matter of talent, but also of respect for the work, for the team, and for the person who will receive what you are making.
When they decided to close the agency, we were all absorbed by WebAr.
Despite the discouragement we felt and the sense of regression we were experiencing, Lucas adapted quickly and continued putting a lot of himself into making things move forward.
That is something else I want to highlight.
Because it is not that hard to push when everything is going well. The difficult thing is to remain available, keep learning, and continue doing things well when the context is not ideal.
Lucas did that.
After two years of working together, deep down I knew Lucas was meant for much more.
Maybe at that moment it was not clear what shape that would take. Maybe [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] was not yet what it would eventually become.

But some signs were already there: the persistence, the speed, the passion for design, the openness to learn, the pursuit of quality, and that ability to keep moving forward even when the scenario changed.
Over time, looking at what he built together with his team, those signs make much more sense.

And it also makes me think about something: many times, we do not know what marks we leave on the people we work with. A correction, a conversation, a way of organizing a problem or sustaining a standard may seem like small things in the moment, but later they travel. They transform. They appear in other places, in other teams, in other cultures.
Maybe leadership is also that.
Not only solving what is happening in the present, but helping shape a way of working that others can carry with them and grow.
Once, during one of those scoldings, I said something to Lucas about his manners when asking for things.
I do not remember the exact reason, although as the conversation was coming to an end, laughing, I said something very inappropriate that I refuse to write here.
You can ask him if he remembers.
Lucas, all the best and congratulations to you and your team.
Here’s to many more years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio].
We invited Nico because he was part of a foundational stage of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], even before [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] existed as a studio.

Back then, Lucas worked with him at WebAr while something that still did not have a clear name was beginning to take shape. Between projects, deadlines, corrections, and everyday learning, Nico was one of those people who helped shape a way of understanding work.

He inspired us because he showed us that leading is also teaching without making too much noise. It is sustaining a standard, correcting with judgment, bringing order when needed, and accompanying others while they are still discovering what they are capable of.
After thinking a lot about my whole journey since that November of 2016, when I joined the studio, I feel there are so many stories to tell.
But when I asked myself what I wanted to share for this invitation, I realized that what marked me the most had more to do with the human side than with design itself.

There was a moment, after several years of working together, when Lucas said something that stayed with me. He told me I was a kind of “invisible leader”: a presence that held things together, but did not need to be at the center.
At the time, I did not think too much about it. To me, I was simply doing my job: supporting a team of designers I trusted deeply.

But over time, I understood that yes, I had always believed that good ideas do not appear when someone tries to control everything. On the contrary, they appear when there is space and trust. When people feel they can try, make mistakes, and try again.

One of the things I enjoyed the most during all those years at the studio was working as a team. Seeing, over and over again, how an idea would appear in a conversation, someone on the team would pick it up, someone else would make it grow, and suddenly something new would start taking shape among everyone, until we reached our beloved “WOW.”
That dynamic of mutual support and trust did not only strengthen the ideas. It also made each person on the team feel part of something bigger.
Over time, I understood that my role was often simply to protect that space. To be available, to support, to motivate, to bring order when needed, and to trust.
For me, leadership is not so much about guiding from the front, but rather from behind. From the kitchen, as I always liked :)
From that place where you support, listen, and trust. A kind of leadership that does not need to occupy the center, but creates the space for others to do so.
I think I also learned that way because it was exactly what they did with me: they gave me space, trust, and freedom to grow.

Because in the end, beyond any brand, project, or design, what we truly build are relationships. Relationships based on trust, respect, and mutual support. Relationships that allow us to grow, learn, and create things that would be difficult to reach alone.
When I look back at this whole journey at [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], that is what I keep: the human side, the bonds, and the trust we built throughout the process.
We invited Mar because she was part of the emotional and creative structure of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] during a fundamental stage of our history.
She was the studio’s first designer. And for nine years, we shared projects, learnings, mistakes, growth, and many decisions that helped us understand what kind of team we wanted to build.

Mar inspired us through the way she showed up. Through her commitment, her calmness, and that rare mix of responsibility and ease. A way of bringing order without making noise, supporting without imposing herself, and holding things together without needing to be at the center.

She also inspired us because, without setting out to do so, she taught us a lot about creative leadership. About giving space, trusting, listening, protecting the process, and understanding that the best ideas often appear when a team feels free to try, make mistakes, and build together.

Over these 20 years of [/nk][https://www.nk.studio], we learned that inspiration does not always come through grand gestures. Sometimes it appears in people who hold things from behind, who create the conditions for others to grow, and who leave a deep mark without making too much noise.
Mar is one of those people.

title: Doing it right even when no one sees it

content: I kept reflecting on this idea of inspiration. What is it? Where does it come from? How is it born?
There is something about inspiration, and about how we built [MANDARiNA][https://www.mandarinacyd.com.ar/], that has always stayed with me.

I started very young. At 19. And I started without knowing anything about branding, without knowing anything about design, without knowing anything about communication. Without knowing anything, basically. I was a blank canvas. I do not come from the classic path of someone who worked for ten or fifteen years at a big agency or studio and then opened something of their own with a structure already learned. Mine was much more intuitive. Much more alive. With the good and the bad. It unfolded as it went.
I built my point of view while looking for references to understand what was possible.

description.description: Marcos, sometime around 2008. A lot of hair, an early Instagram filter, and the same logo [Mandarina][https://www.mandarinacyd.com.ar/] has been using for the past 23 years.

content: As I got to know studios, people, brands, campaigns, and clients, I became more and more inspired. I had to nourish myself with everything and everyone, because I literally started from zero. It was not passive inspiration. It was not simply looking at beautiful things. It was an inspiration that pushed me. That made me uncomfortable. That constantly made me ask myself whether we could do better.
And I think that was always the engine behind [MANDARiNA][https://www.mandarinacyd.com.ar/].
That capacity for wonder.
That constant search.
That hunger.
Because for something to inspire you, you first have to be searching. Searching for ideas, searching for quality, searching for a better version of what you do. And that is how we always worked.
Again and again, we would look at work from other studios or agencies and say:
“Honestly, these people are doing something better than us.”
And far from paralyzing us, that activated us.
We always had the humility to recognize when someone was above us. But we also had the obsession of wanting to get there. To work harder. To raise our standard. To constantly iterate on our own work.
For us, inspiration was never empty admiration.
It was fuel.
And there is another story that, for me, explains a lot about how we understand the craft.

Many years ago, I read an anecdote about Steve Jobs. He told the story of his father, who was a carpenter, building a piece of furniture. There was a back part, an internal part, that was going to be completely against the wall. No one would see it.
His father still took the time to make it impeccable.
Steve Jobs said something like:
“But no one is going to see it.”
And his father replied:
“You will.”
That idea always stayed with me.
Because it is not about perfectionism. It is about integrity.
It is about doing things well even when no one is watching.
About understanding that the real standard is not external. It does not depend on awards, likes, or recognition. It depends on the relationship you have with the work.

And I deeply believe in that. Especially because I think our industry has a lot of that “no one is going to see it” mindset, since many clients often have no idea about design, branding, or strategy. Many times, when my team says, “but the client loved it,” I insist that the bar has to be ours, not the client’s. In general, the client does not know or does not fully understand.
True quality appears in the parts no one sees.
In the invisible details.
In the strategy behind the aesthetics.
In the internal logic.
In the obsession with detail.
In the versions that are never shown.
In the neatness.
In the dedication.
In doing things well even if no one is going to notice.
Because in the end, craft is defined there.
In the back of the piece of furniture.
And perhaps that was always [MANDARiNA][https://www.mandarinacyd.com.ar/]:
a mix of hunger and integrity.
The constant search for inspiration in order to grow.

And the obsession with doing things well even when no one is seeing them. And today, in a world of AI, acceleration, and efficiency, what moves us is ultimately the opposite. The good, the beautiful, the things that take time.

And to be clear, we do not have it all figured out. It gets harder and harder, and it hurts more and more, but at the same time we have never been clearer about it. I think that is our inspiration: to make work that is REALLY good, work that keeps getting better.
Good work inspires.
Always.

We invited Marcos because, for many years, [Mandarina][https://www.mandarinacyd.com.ar/] was a concrete reference for [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] of what could be built from Argentina with judgment, consistency, and ambition.

When [/nk][https://www.nk.studio] was still finding its shape, looking at [Mandarina][https://www.mandarinacyd.com.ar/] meant looking toward a north star. A studio creating brands with personality, projects with craft, and work that showed us that you did not need to be somewhere else in the world to do things well, seriously, and with a point of view of your own.
Marcos inspired us through that rare mix of hunger and integrity. Hunger to always search for a better version of the work. Integrity to uphold the standard even when no one is watching.

Over time, that admiration became something closer: conversations, friendship, camaraderie, and a shared perspective on what it means to sustain a studio. To grow, make mistakes, insist, try again, and keep defending quality even when the context pushes in the opposite direction.

His story captures something we also feel deeply: inspiration is not looking at something from afar. It is allowing it to move you. To make you uncomfortable. To force you to ask yourself whether you can do better.
Marcos inspires us because he reminds us that craft is tested in the back of the piece of furniture. In what is not always seen, but defines who you are.
